title: Evaluating the Effect of Activity-Based Method of Teaching Mathematics on Nigerian Secondary School Students’ Achievement in Mathematics
extended_summary:
This paper addresses poor achievement in secondary school mathematics and asks whether an activity-based teaching method can improve students’ mathematics performance compared with the lecture method. The motivation is the persistent low performance of Nigerian students in mathematics and the need for more effective classroom pedagogy.

The study tested an activity-based instructional approach against a lecture-based approach in the topics of circle geometry and construction. It used a pretest-posttest quasi-experimental design with intact classes, analyzing outcomes with ANCOVA to control for pretest scores. The intervention was delivered to Senior Secondary II students in two government-owned schools in Calabar Metropolis, Cross River State, Nigeria.

A sample of 96 students participated, split evenly between the experimental and control groups. The main finding was that students taught with the activity-based method scored significantly higher on the posttest than those taught with the lecture method, even after controlling for pretest performance. The paper concludes that activity-based learning is more effective for improving mathematics achievement in this context and recommends training teachers to use it more widely.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design with a comparison group and ANCOVA adjustment for pretest, which gives moderate credibility. However, it is not randomized at the individual level, uses intact classes from only two schools, and reports no confidence intervals.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported group effect is large (partial η²=0.261), exceeding the threshold for medium/large impact. The finding suggests a strong positive effect on mathematics achievement in a priority population, even though the intervention is pedagogical rather than technology-based.

finding.finding_summary: In a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest study with intact classes (n=96; 48 activity-based, 48 lecture), students taught with the activity-based method scored substantially higher on the mathematics posttest than those taught with lecture after controlling for pretest performance. The adjusted group effect was significant in ANCOVA, F(1,93)=114.461, p<0.001, with partial eta squared η²=0.261, indicating the activity-based approach explained 26.1% of posttest variance.
finding.measure: 20-item Mathematics Test (essay test) on circle geometry and construction; pretest and posttest achievement scores
